parts.title: Enrolling on a photography course
parts.intro: You will hear a man phoning an arts centre to enrol on an evening course.

script.t: Good afternoon, Westfield Arts Centre. This is Claire. How can I help?
Hi. I saw your leaflet about evening courses and I’d like to enrol on one of the photography classes.
Lovely. I can do that for you now over the phone. Can I take your name first?
Yes, it’s Robert Thorley. That’s T, H, O, R, L, E, Y.
Thank you, Mr Thorley. And your address?
Eighteen Cobden Street. C, O, B, D, E, N. It’s here in Westfield.
script.say: Eighteen Cobden Street. C, O, B, D, E, N. It’s here in Westfield.

script.t: Got that. Now, we run two photography courses this term. There’s one for beginners and an intermediate one.
I did wonder about the intermediate course because I’ve read quite a lot about photography. But to be honest, I’ve only ever used my phone. I’ve never had a proper camera.
Then I’d definitely recommend the course for beginners. The intermediate group are already confident with all the manual settings.
Yes, I think that makes sense. Put me down for that one.
Now, the leaflet says the beginners’ class is on Monday evenings, but I’m afraid that’s changed. The tutor can’t do Mondays any more, so it’s moved to Wednesdays.
Wednesday is actually better for me, so that’s fine.
Good. And the first session is on the third of October.
The third? I thought it said the tenth on the website.
Let me check. Oh, you’re right, sorry. The third was the start date last year. It’s Wednesday the 10th of October.
script.say: Let me check. Oh, you’re right, sorry. The third was the start date last year. It’s Wednesday the tenth of October.

script.t: OK. And how much is the course?
It’s £120 for the ten weeks. If you become a member of the arts centre, it’s £95, but membership costs £40 a year.
script.say: It’s a hundred and twenty pounds for the ten weeks. If you become a member of the arts centre, it’s ninety-five, but membership costs forty pounds a year.

script.t: Well, I don’t think I’ll be doing any other courses this year, so it’s not worth it for me. I’ll just pay the full price.
No problem.
Now, I’ll just tell you what you need to bring. Obviously you need a camera. It doesn’t have to be an expensive one.
I’m borrowing my brother’s. Does it matter what kind?
Not really. But make sure you bring a spare memory card, because you’ll be taking a lot of pictures, and the tutor will want to look at them in class.
Right. Should I bring a laptop too?
No, there are computers in the room. But do bring a notebook. Most people find it helpful to write down the settings they’ve used.
OK. And is it all in the classroom?

Mostly, but in week six there’s a trip. It used to be to the castle, but the castle is closed for repairs this year, so the group will go down to the harbour instead. It’s great for photographing boats and the evening light.
That sounds good. One last thing: where can I park?
The car park at the front is for staff only, I’m afraid. But you can park for free in the car park behind the library. It’s just two minutes’ walk.
Perfect. Thanks very much for your help.
You’re welcome. See you in October.

parts.title: Volunteering at a nature reserve
parts.intro: You will hear a talk given to new volunteers at a nature reserve.

script.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Marshfield Nature Reserve. My name’s Tom Fielding and I manage the volunteer programme here. Thank you all for giving up your time.

Let me start with a little background. Many people think the reserve has always been protected wetland, but in fact, until about forty years ago, this whole area was used for digging gravel. When the gravel company left, the pits filled with water, and that’s how the lakes you see today were formed.
Today the reserve is owned by a wildlife trust. The local council gives us a small grant each year, but most of our money comes from membership fees and the café.

We have around a hundred and twenty volunteers. Some of you may be wondering how much time you need to give. We don’t ask for a minimum number of hours. What we do ask is that you let us know at least a week in advance which days you’re coming, so we can plan the work.

Now, safety. All the tools are provided, and you’ll get gloves. The thing I really must stress, though, is the water. Some of the lakes are very deep close to the edge, so please never work near the water on your own. Always have a partner with you.
As a thank-you, volunteers get free parking and a discount in the café. And every December we have a dinner for all our volunteers, which is always a great evening.

Something else you might be pleased to hear: after six months, volunteers can take part in our training courses, completely free. Last year, people learned how to identify birds, and others did a first-aid course. We also give a certificate that many of you might find useful when applying for jobs.
Right, let me tell you about the different jobs we need help with. You can choose what suits you.

First, the bird survey. This involves counting the birds on the main lake once a month. You don’t need to be an expert, as you’ll always be with an experienced counter, but you do need to arrive early, because we start at half past six in the morning.

Then there’s path maintenance. This means cutting back plants and repairing the paths after the winter. It can be quite hard physical work, so it’s not for everyone, but people who do it say it keeps them fit.

The visitor centre is where we welcome the public and answer questions. It’s indoors, so it’s a good choice in bad weather. The main thing is that you need to enjoy talking to people; you don’t need any special knowledge because we give you an information pack.

Finally, school visits. Groups of children come to us most weeks during term time, and volunteers help lead the activities, like pond dipping. Because you’ll be working with children, you’ll need to have a background check before you start, which takes about a month.
So, have a think about which of these you’d like to do, and we’ll talk to each of you after the coffee break.

parts.title: Planning a presentation on sleep
parts.intro: You will hear two students, Hannah and Leo, talking to their tutor about a presentation on sleep and learning.

script.t: So, Hannah and Leo, how’s the presentation on sleep and learning coming along?

Quite well, I think. We’ve done most of the reading. At first we were going to focus on how much sleep teenagers need, but there’s already so much on that, so we decided to look at how sleep affects memory instead.
Good, that’s more focused. What was the most surprising thing you found?
For me, it was that the brain actually replays what we’ve learned during the day while we sleep. I knew sleep was important, but I hadn’t realised it was such an active process.
I was more surprised by how quickly the effects appear. Just one night without enough sleep can reduce the ability to form new memories by about forty per cent.
That’s a striking figure. Make sure you give the source for it. Now, how are you going to start the presentation?
I wanted to start with a lot of statistics, but Hannah thought that might be boring.
I suggested we begin by asking the audience how many hours they slept last night. It gets everyone involved straight away.
I agree with Hannah. A question to the audience works well. You can bring in the statistics later. What about visuals?
We have some graphs, but they’re quite complicated.
Then I’d simplify them. One clear message per slide. Your audience won’t have time to read small labels.
OK. And we were thinking of doing a little memory test with the class at the end.

That’s a nice idea, but be careful with time. You only have fifteen minutes, and the test could easily take five. I’d suggest you put it in the middle, where it can illustrate a point, rather than at the end when you may be running out of time.
Now, let’s look at the studies you’ve chosen. What did you think of the one with the medical students?
It was interesting, but it only had twelve participants. So I don’t think we can draw strong conclusions from it.
Fair point. And the study on napping?
That one I really liked. It showed that even a twenty-minute nap improved test scores. And it’s something students can actually do, so it’s really practical.
And the study about phone use at night?
We’re not sure about that one. The researchers worked for a company that sells sleep apps, so they might not be completely neutral.
It’s good that you noticed that. What about the Japanese study?
It was really detailed, but it’s twenty-five years old. Things have changed a lot since then, especially with phones and screens, so it might be out of date.
And finally, the large survey from Canada?
That was the best one, I think. Over ten thousand students took part, so the results are much more reliable than the others.
Good. I think you’ve got a clear picture. Let’s meet again next week.

parts.title: The history of glass
parts.intro: You will hear part of a lecture about the history of glass.

script.t: This afternoon I’m going to talk about one of the most useful materials ever invented: glass. We use it every day, in windows, bottles and screens, but its history goes back thousands of years.

Glass is made mainly from sand, which is heated until it melts. On its own, sand needs an extremely high temperature to melt, so early glassmakers added a substance called soda, which lowered the melting point. Lime was also added to make the glass stronger and stop it dissolving in water.

The earliest glass objects we know of are beads, which were made in Mesopotamia around four and a half thousand years ago. At first, glass was so rare that it was treated like a precious stone, and only the very rich could afford it.
For centuries, glass vessels were made by shaping melted glass around a core of clay and sand, which was removed once the glass had cooled. This was slow work, and each piece took many hours.

The great breakthrough came about two thousand years ago, probably on the coast of what is now Syria, with the invention of glassblowing. A worker blew air through a metal tube into a ball of hot glass, making it expand like a balloon. Suddenly, vessels could be made quickly, glass became cheap, and it was soon an everyday material across the Roman Empire.
The Romans were also the first to use glass in windows, although their windows were small and not very clear. You could see light through them, but not much detail.

In the Middle Ages, the city of Venice became the centre of European glassmaking. In 1291, the glassmakers were all moved to the island of Murano. The official reason was to reduce the risk of fire in the city, as glass furnaces burned day and night. But it also made it easier to keep the techniques secret.
script.say: In the Middle Ages, the city of Venice became the centre of European glassmaking. In twelve ninety-one, the glassmakers were all moved to the island of Murano. The official reason was to reduce the risk of fire in the city, as glass furnaces burned day and night. But it also made it easier to keep the techniques secret.

script.t: Venetian glassmakers developed a very clear glass known as cristallo, and they also produced high-quality mirrors, which were sold all over Europe for enormous prices.

In the seventeenth century, an English glassmaker called George Ravenscroft discovered that adding lead to glass made it heavier and more brilliant. This lead crystal was perfect for cutting into decorative shapes, and it soon became fashionable for drinking glasses.

Making large, flat sheets of glass for windows remained difficult until the 1950s, when Alastair Pilkington developed the float process. In this method, melted glass is poured onto a bath of liquid tin. The glass floats on the surface and spreads out to form a perfectly flat sheet. Almost all window glass is still made this way today.
script.say: Making large, flat sheets of glass for windows remained difficult until the nineteen fifties, when Alastair Pilkington developed the float process. In this method, melted glass is poured onto a bath of liquid tin. The glass floats on the surface and spreads out to form a perfectly flat sheet. Almost all window glass is still made this way today.

script.t: Finally, glass is also excellent for the environment in one important way: it can be recycled again and again without losing quality. Recycled glass melts at a lower temperature than raw materials, so using it saves energy.
And modern research continues. Today, thin glass fibres carry internet data around the world as pulses of light, so glass, one of our oldest materials, is now at the heart of our newest technology.
